questions.q: Per this lesson, how does a target-state vision differ from a detailed design?
options: A vision specifies outcomes, while a detailed design specifies things like object names, sharing rules, and integration patterns
A vision is always longer and more technical than a detailed design
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
A vision is written only after the detailed design is finished and approved
questions.explain: A target-state vision is a short, outcome-level statement written before the detailed design, so later design decisions have something to be checked against — it deliberately avoids specifying design details.

questions.q: Why would a vision promising 'real-time integration with every system in the landscape' actually be a worse vision, per this lesson?
options: Because real-time integration is never achievable with any Salesforce implementation
Because it would promise something LedgerPoint, per Lesson 4's constraints, structurally cannot deliver, setting the design up to fail its own stated goal
Because Architecture Review Boards always reject ambitious visions on principle
Because dealers and end customers do not want real-time integration
questions.explain: Lesson 4 already established LedgerPoint has no modern API and is batch-only; a vision promising uniform real-time integration ignores that constraint and sets the design up to fail against its own stated commitment.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the six capabilities LTV Global's target-state vision commits to?
options: Replacing Meridian ERP with a new cloud-native system
A unified customer view across all four business units and three regions
Eliminating the need for any identity provider
Full real-time integration with LedgerPoint
questions.explain: A unified customer view is one of the six named commitments, mapped forward to the data architecture lesson; the vision does not promise ERP replacement, eliminating identity providers, or real-time LedgerPoint integration.

questions.q: What does 'sustainable governance,' the sixth capability in the vision, specifically commit to?
options: Governance that requires no documentation at all
A governance model designed so that one engagement team member leaving doesn't put the system at risk
A governance model that only applies during the initial build phase
Governance handled entirely by an external vendor with no internal involvement
questions.explain: The vision explicitly commits to a solution governed, deployed, and maintained in a way that survives individual staff turnover, not one that depends on a single person's memory.

questions.q: The lesson says a vision statement that is 'vague enough that almost any design could claim to satisfy it' has what problem?
options: It is too detailed and functions as a disguised solution design
It isn't actually doing the job a vision is supposed to do
It is the correct and desired level of detail for a target-state vision
It should be rewritten as a requirement instead of a vision
questions.explain: The lesson states that if a vision is vague enough that almost any design could claim to satisfy it, it isn't doing its job of giving later design decisions something concrete to be checked against.
